0.title: Words That Wound and Words That Heal
0.overview:
Most of us speak thousands of words every day, and type thousands more. We rarely stop to think how much those words matter. Yet Scripture says, Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Prov 18:21). A single sentence can crush a child's spirit or lift a friend out of despair. Words can start wars, end marriages, destroy reputations, and also bring comfort, peace and the good news of salvation.

Jesus said our words reveal our hearts: For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt 12:34). And he warned that we will give account for them: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak (Matt 12:36). That is a sobering thought for anyone who has ever said something they regret, which is everyone.

This study looks at the power of words, the many ways the tongue sins, the words that build others up, the art of speaking truth in love and how God tames the tongue by changing the heart. Everything here applies equally to emails, messages and social media, where many of today's most careless words are written.

Five units: (1) The Power of Words; (2) Sins of the Tongue; (3) Words That Build Up; (4) Speaking the Truth in Love; (5) Taming the Tongue.

1.title: The Power of Words
1.overview:
God speaks. The Bible opens with God speaking the world into existence: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light (Gen 1:3). God's words create, command, promise and save. His Son is called the Word (John 1:1). Made in his image, human beings are speaking creatures. Our words carry a reflection of God's creative power, for good or ill.

A small member with great power. James uses vivid pictures. The tongue is like a bit in a horse's mouth or a rudder on a ship: small, but it steers the whole. It is like a spark that sets a forest ablaze: How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire (Jas 3:5-6). One careless remark can spread destruction far beyond what we intended.

Untameable by human effort. For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison (Jas 3:7-8). We can train animals but not our own mouths. This is humbling, and it drives us to God.

Words reveal the heart. Jesus taught that the tongue is not the root problem but the outflow. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil (Matt 12:35). Harsh words come from a harsh heart; lying words from a deceitful heart; complaining words from a discontented heart. To change our speech, we need changed hearts.

Words will be judged. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned (Matt 12:37). Our words are evidence of what is in us. God hears every word, including the ones spoken in private or typed anonymously.

Inconsistency. James notes the strange inconsistency of the tongue: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God (Jas 3:9). We sing praises on Sunday and speak cruelly at home on Monday. My brothers, these things ought not to be so (Jas 3:10).
1.theology:
Words and the image of God: James grounds his rebuke in the fact that people are made in God's likeness. To curse a human being is to dishonour the image of God. This is why insults, mockery and contempt are serious sins (Matt 5:22).

Teachers' greater accountability: James begins his discussion with a warning: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (Jas 3:1). Those whose words reach many have greater responsibility.

Words that save: God has chosen to save people through words, the preaching of the gospel (Rom 10:14-17). The tongue that can destroy can also proclaim eternal life.
1.examples:
Then: Rehoboam, Solomon's son, was asked by the people to lighten their burdens. Older advisers urged him to speak kindly; younger ones urged harshness. He answered harshly, and ten tribes broke away from his kingdom (1 Kgs 12:13-16). A few harsh words divided a nation.

Now: A father, frustrated after a long day, tells his teenage son, "You'll never amount to anything." He forgets it the next day. His son remembers it for twenty years. When the father finally realises, he asks his son's forgiveness, and they both weep.

A simple test: Think back over the words you spoke or wrote yesterday. Which did the most good? Which did the most harm?

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness. For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body. If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs. So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James warns teachers, then widens his warning to all. Everyone stumbles in many ways, and the person who never stumbles in speech is perfect. The tongue is small but powerful, like a bit, a rudder or a spark. It can set the whole course of life on fire. Few passages in Scripture describe a sin so vividly.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so. Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Humanity has tamed every kind of animal but cannot tame the tongue. It blesses God and curses people made in his image. James uses images from nature: a spring cannot pour out both fresh and salt water; a fig tree cannot bear olives. A consistent life produces consistent speech.

verseByVerse.quote: "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, who had just accused him of being in league with Satan. A tree is known by its fruit, and a person by their words. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. And everyone will give account for every careless word. Our speech is a window into our souls.

verseByVerse.quote: From the fruit of a man's mouth his stomach is satisfied; he is satisfied by the yield of his lips. Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs pictures words as fruit that fills the stomach. What we say comes back to us. Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love to use it will eat its fruit. We reap what we speak.

1.reflection:
Why does James say the tongue is impossible for humans to tame?

What do your words over the last week reveal about your heart?

Can you remember words spoken to you that still affect you, for good or harm?

How does the truth that you will give account for every careless word change how you speak?

2.title: Sins of the Tongue
2.overview:
Scripture names many sins of speech. Seeing them clearly helps us recognise them in ourselves.

Lying. Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another (Eph 4:25). Lying includes outright falsehood, half-truths, exaggeration and creating false impressions. The devil is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). God is truth.

Gossip and slander. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered (Prov 11:13). Gossip spreads private information to people who do not need it. Slander spreads false or damaging information to harm someone's reputation. Both destroy trust and divide friends. For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases (Prov 26:20).

Harsh and angry words. A harsh word stirs up anger (Prov 15:1). Jesus taught that calling someone a fool in anger is a serious sin (Matt 5:22). Shouting, insulting and belittling words wound deeply.

Complaining and grumbling. Do all things without grumbling or disputing (Phil 2:14). Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and God took it as rebellion against him (Num 14:27). Constant complaining spreads discontent and shows a lack of trust in God's goodness.

Flattery. A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet (Prov 29:5). Flattery is insincere praise used to manipulate. It is a kind of lying.

Boasting. Speaking to make ourselves look good, exaggerating our achievements or dropping names, comes from pride.

Crude and coarse talk. Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving (Eph 5:4). Coarse humour and obscene language dishonour God and cheapen what is precious.

Too many words. When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent (Prov 10:19). Sometimes the sin is simply talking too much, not listening and filling silence with careless words.
2.theology:
The ninth commandment: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor (Exod 20:16). This commandment forbids not only lying in court but every word that harms a neighbour's reputation unjustly. It also requires us to defend others' good names.

Gossip disguised as concern: Christians sometimes spread gossip under the cover of "prayer requests" or "concern." Before sharing information about someone, ask: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? Would I say it in their presence?

Online speech: Social media amplifies every sin of the tongue. Anonymity, speed and distance make people say things they would never say face to face. The same rules apply online as everywhere else.
2.examples:
Then: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, partly because of his wife and partly from jealousy. God heard it and struck Miriam with leprosy. Moses, the one wronged, prayed for her healing (Num 12:1-13). God takes slander of his servants seriously.

Now: A group of church members often meets for coffee, and conversation regularly turns to criticism of other members. One woman realises that she leaves every time feeling worse about her church. She decides to steer conversations in a different direction and, when necessary, to say gently, "I don't think we should talk about her when she's not here." Others are relieved.

A simple test: Which sin of the tongue are you most prone to? Ask someone close to you; they probably know.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another. Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil. Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul lists sins of speech to put away: falsehood, corrupting talk, bitterness, clamour, slander. He replaces them with truth, words that build up and kindness. Notice the reason for truthfulness: we are members one of another. Lying to a fellow believer is like one part of the body deceiving another.

verseByVerse.quote: For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife. The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body. Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart. Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart; though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs gives a cluster of warnings about whispering, quarrelling and deceitful speech. Gossip is like delicious food that goes deep into the body. Smooth words can hide a hateful heart. A lying tongue hates its victims. The wise see through flattering speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul calls believers to do everything without grumbling or disputing. The result: they will be blameless, shining as lights in a crooked generation. A Christian who does not complain stands out. Contentment in speech is itself a witness to God's goodness.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool. When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These proverbs contrast the fool's speech and the righteous person's speech. Hiding hatred with lying lips and spreading slander are folly. Many words lead to sin; restraint is wise. The tongue of the righteous is like choice silver, and its words nourish many.

2.reflection:
Which sin of the tongue described in this unit are you most prone to?

How do you tell the difference between sharing a concern and gossip?

Why does Paul connect truthfulness to being "members one of another"?

What would change in your online speech if you applied these principles?

3.title: Words That Build Up
3.overview:
The tongue is not only dangerous. It is also one of the greatest instruments of good. The same mouth that can wound can heal.

Words that give grace. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear (Eph 4:29). Paul's test for our words is threefold: Do they build up? Do they fit the occasion? Do they give grace? Words can be channels of God's grace to others.

Gentle answers. A soft answer turns away wrath (Prov 15:1). In conflict, a gentle tone often calms what a sharp one would inflame.

Encouragement. Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing (1 Thess 5:11). Barnabas, whose name means "son of encouragement" according to Acts 4:36, saw the good in people others doubted, such as the newly converted Saul and the young John Mark. A word of encouragement can change the course of someone's life.

Kind and timely words. Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body (Prov 16:24). A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver (Prov 25:11). The right word at the right moment is a rare and beautiful gift.

Gratitude. Paul replaces crude talk with thanksgiving (Eph 5:4). Thanking God and thanking others transforms the atmosphere of a home, a workplace or a church.

Gospel words. The greatest words we can speak are words about Christ. How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news! (Rom 10:15). Every Christian can speak of what Christ has done for them.

Gracious and seasoned. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person (Col 4:6). Gracious speech is not bland. Salt gives flavour and preserves. Christian speech should be kind, thoughtful and interesting.
3.theology:
Blessing: Scripture often speaks of blessing others with words. Parents blessed children; priests blessed the people (Num 6:24-26). Christians are called to bless even those who curse them (Luke 6:28). Speaking blessing reflects the heart of God, who blesses.

Encouragement is a ministry: Some believers have a particular gift of encouragement (Rom 12:8), but all are called to encourage one another daily (Heb 3:13).

The model of Christ: People marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth (Luke 4:22). He spoke truth with perfect grace. He knew when to rebuke and when to comfort, when to speak and when to be silent.
3.examples:
Then: When the newly converted Saul came to Jerusalem, the disciples were afraid of him. Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (Acts 9:26-27). A few words from Barnabas opened the door for the greatest missionary in history.

Now: A teacher writes a short note to a struggling student, telling her she has a gift for writing. Years later, that student, now an author, says the note was the reason she kept going. The teacher had forgotten writing it.

A simple test: Who could you encourage today with a specific, sincere word?

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul forbids corrupting talk, words that are rotten and spread decay. Instead, our words should build up, fit the moment and give grace. Then he adds: do not grieve the Holy Spirit. Our speech affects not only others but the Spirit who lives in us. Harsh words grieve him; gracious words please him.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A soft answer turns away wrath; a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge; the mouth of fools pours out folly. A gentle tongue is a tree of life. Our tone often matters as much as our words.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness. Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly. The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips. Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness. The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious. Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healthy to the body. Kind words have physical, emotional and spiritual effects.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul tells believers to walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Their speech should always be gracious and seasoned with salt, so that they know how to answer each person. Our conversations with unbelievers are opportunities for the gospel.

3.reflection:
Apply Paul's threefold test in Ephesians 4:29 to a recent conversation.

Who has spoken words of encouragement that shaped your life?

How could you speak more gratitude in your home or workplace?

What does it mean for speech to be "seasoned with salt"?

4.title: Speaking the Truth in Love
4.overview:
Two errors are common in Christian speech. Some speak truth without love: they are blunt, critical and harsh, and they call it honesty. Others speak love without truth: they flatter, avoid hard conversations and never say anything difficult, and they call it kindness. Paul calls us to something better: speaking the truth in love (Eph 4:15).

Truth matters. God hates lying, and love does not pretend. Better is open rebuke than hidden love (Prov 27:5). Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Prov 27:6). A friend who never tells us hard truths is not really a friend. Nathan's rebuke to David, You are the man!, was an act of love that led to repentance (2 Sam 12:7).

Love matters. Truth without love is a weapon. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing (Prov 12:18). Love chooses the right time, the right place, the right tone and the right words. It speaks privately before publicly. It speaks to help, not to win.

Gentle correction. Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Gal 6:1). Correction should be gentle, humble and aimed at restoration.

Listening first. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger (Jas 1:19). Many conflicts would be avoided if we listened carefully before speaking. If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame (Prov 18:13).

Receiving truth. Speaking truth in love also includes receiving it. Humble Christians welcome correction, even when it stings. Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it (Ps 141:5).
4.theology:
Christ's example: Jesus spoke hard truths to the Pharisees, to Peter and to the rich young ruler. But Mark says of the rich young man, And Jesus, looking at him, loved him (Mark 10:21), before telling him what he needed to hear. Truth and love were perfectly joined in Christ.

Growing up into Christ: Paul says that speaking the truth in love is how the church grows up into Christ (Eph 4:15). Healthy churches are places of honest, loving conversation, not flattery or harshness.

Conflict: Jesus' instructions in Matthew 18:15-17 show a pattern for addressing sin: privately first, then with witnesses, then with the church. Most conflicts should be resolved at the first step, with honest, gentle speech.
4.examples:
Then: When Peter, under pressure, withdrew from eating with Gentile believers, Paul opposed him to his face (Gal 2:11). It was a hard conversation, but the gospel was at stake. Later Peter spoke of our beloved brother Paul (2 Pet 3:15). Truth spoken in love did not end their friendship.

Now: A woman notices that her friend has become bitter and sharp-tongued since a family conflict. She is tempted to say nothing. Instead, she prays, chooses a quiet moment and says, "I love you, and I'm worried. Can I share something I've noticed?" Her friend is hurt at first, then grateful. It becomes a turning point.

A simple test: Do you tend more toward truth without love, or love without truth?

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes. Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God gives the church teachers to equip believers for ministry, so that the church grows to maturity and is not tossed about by false teaching. The means of growth is speaking the truth in love. Every member contributes to building up the body in love. Honest, loving speech is how churches mature.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Open rebuke is better than hidden love. The wounds of a friend are faithful; the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. True friends tell us hard things, because they love us. Flatterers tell us what we want to hear, and it may be because they do not care.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James gives a simple formula: quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Human anger does not produce God's righteousness. Instead, believers should receive God's word with meekness. Listening to God and listening to others go together.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment. Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs contrasts truthful and deceitful speech. Rash words pierce like swords; wise words bring healing. Truthful lips endure forever; a lying tongue lasts only a moment. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight.

4.reflection:
Do you tend toward truth without love or love without truth? How can you grow?

Is there a hard but loving conversation you have been avoiding?

How well do you receive correction? Think of a recent example.

Read James 1:19. Which of the three is hardest for you?

5.title: Taming the Tongue
5.overview:
If no human being can tame the tongue (Jas 3:8), is there any hope? Yes, because God can. He changes our speech by changing our hearts.

A new heart. Since the mouth speaks from the heart, the first step is a heart renewed by the gospel. Isaiah, seeing God's holiness, cried, I am a man of unclean lips (Isa 6:5). A seraph touched his lips with a burning coal from the altar and said, your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for (Isa 6:7). Cleansed lips come from atonement. The more we treasure Christ, the more our words will reflect him.

Prayer for our speech. Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! (Ps 141:3). Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer (Ps 19:14). Praying before conversations, meetings and difficult phone calls invites God's help.

Filling the heart with God's word. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Col 3:16). When Scripture fills our hearts, it shapes our words. Memorising Scripture gives us better things to say.

The value of silence. Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise (Prov 17:28). Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble (Prov 21:23). Sometimes the most godly thing we can do is say nothing. Waiting before replying, especially in anger or online, prevents many sins.

Confession and repair. When we sin with our words, we should confess quickly to God and to those we have hurt. "I was wrong to say that. Will you forgive me?" Words that wounded can be followed by words that heal.

Practical habits. Pause before speaking when angry. Do not send a message written in anger until you have slept on it. Before passing on news about someone, ask whether it is true, necessary and kind. Speak about people as if they were present. Look for one person to encourage each day.
5.theology:
The Spirit and speech: Self-control, gentleness and kindness are fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22-23). The Spirit who lives in believers produces new speech. We cooperate by putting off the old and putting on the new.

Perfect speech in glory: James says that whoever never stumbles in speech is a perfect man (Jas 3:2). No one achieves that in this life. But in glory, our speech will be perfectly holy, and every word will praise God and bless others. The redeemed will sing the new song (Rev 5:9).

Forgiveness for the tongue: Every Christian has sinned with their tongue countless times. Christ's blood covers those sins too. We fight sins of speech not to earn forgiveness but because we have received it.
5.examples:
Then: Peter's tongue got him into trouble repeatedly: rebuking Jesus, boasting he would never deny him, then denying him with curses (Mark 8:32; 14:29, 71). After Pentecost, filled with the Spirit, the same tongue preached Christ boldly to thousands (Acts 2). God tamed Peter's tongue and used it.

Now: A man known for his sharp tongue at work starts praying Psalm 141:3 every morning. He also makes a rule: when he feels angry in a meeting, he waits ten seconds before speaking. Over months, colleagues notice the change. One asks him what happened. He tells her about Christ.

A simple test: What one practical habit could you adopt this week to guard your tongue?

verseByVerse.quote: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it. Yet my prayer is continually against their evil deeds. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David asks God to set a guard on his mouth and keep watch over his lips. He prays that his heart will not incline to evil. And he welcomes rebuke from the righteous as a kindness. Guarding the tongue begins with prayer and humility.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!" Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah saw the holy God and immediately became aware of his unclean lips and his people's unclean lips. The seraph touched his lips with a coal from the altar, the place of sacrifice. Guilt removed, sin atoned for. Then Isaiah was ready to speak for God. Our lips are cleansed by the sacrifice of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression. Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David ends his great psalm about God's word with a prayer. He asks to be kept from hidden faults and presumptuous sins. Then he prays that his words and meditations will be acceptable to God, his rock and redeemer. Words that please God come from a heart shaped by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: "For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus repeats the principle: a good tree bears good fruit; a bad tree bears bad fruit. The good person brings good out of the good treasure of the heart. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. To change our words, God must change our hearts. And he does.

5.reflection:
Pray Psalm 141:3 and Psalm 19:14 each morning this week. What difference does it make?

When is silence the wisest response for you?

Is there someone you need to ask forgiveness for words you spoke?

How does Isaiah 6:5-7 show where clean speech comes from?
